nameStory: This plant gets its "four o'clock" name because its funnel-shaped flowers have a very particular schedule - they open in late afternoon around 4 PM and close again after just a few hours. It's like nature's own timekeeper! The "wild" part distinguishes it from its showier garden cousin, the Marvel of Peru, which follows the same punctual blooming habit.
description: Wild four o'clock is a sturdy perennial herb that can grow over three feet tall with a distinctly upright, branching growth habit. The plant has a somewhat weedy appearance with heart-shaped leaves arranged in pairs along the lower stems. Its most notable feature is clusters of small, funnel-shaped flowers in shades of magenta, pink, or white that bloom briefly in late afternoon. This native wildflower has a thick, fleshy taproot that helps it survive in tough conditions.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small funnel-shaped flowers about half an inch wide bloom in tight clusters of 3-5, surrounded by a cup-like cluster of papery bracts. Colors range from bright magenta to pale pink or white, and they only open for a few hours in late afternoon.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped to oval leaves grow in opposite pairs, feeling thin and somewhat papery to the touch. Each leaf can be up to 4 inches long and has smooth edges with prominent veining.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Erect plant that branches into a distinctive Y-shaped fork pattern in the upper portions where flowers appear. The stem can feel slightly hairy or completely smooth depending on the individual plant.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: After flowers drop, small hairy fruits develop inside the persistent papery bracts, creating clusters that look shaggy and cup-shaped. The dried fruit clusters rattle softly when shaken.

idTips.label: Root
idTips.description: Has a thick, fleshy taproot that can be quite substantial - much larger than you'd expect for the size of the above-ground plant.

habitat: Look for wild four o'clock in disturbed areas like roadsides, vacant lots, field edges, and waste places throughout New England. It thrives in poor, dry soils and sunny locations where other plants struggle. This adaptable species often pops up in gardens as a volunteer, spreading easily into areas with loose or recently disturbed soil.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from the thick taproot, with young heart-shaped leaves appearing in opposite pairs along reddish stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season when the distinctive late-afternoon flower show occurs daily. Look for the Y-shaped branching pattern and flower clusters in leaf joints.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue blooming until frost, while papery seed cups become more prominent. Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to the ground, with only the thick taproot surviving underground until spring.

funFact: This plant is a living clock that you can actually use to tell time! The flowers are so reliable in their late-afternoon opening schedule that indigenous peoples and early settlers would use them as a natural timepiece, knowing it was around 4 PM when the blooms opened.
confusionNotes: The heart-shaped leaves might be confused with morning glories, but wild four o'clock grows upright rather than vining, and its flowers are much smaller and bloom in tight clusters rather than singly. Remember: four o'clocks stand up straight, morning glories climb around.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this native wildflower with the popular garden plant called Marvel of Peru or garden four o'clock - they're close relatives but the garden variety has much showier, larger flowers and is originally from South America. Both follow the same late-day blooming schedule though!
compareHints: Wild four o'clock is much less showy than its garden relative Marvel of Peru, with smaller flowers (about half an inch vs. 2 inches wide) and a more weedy appearance. While Marvel of Peru has bold, trumpet-like blooms, wild four o'clock's flowers are modest and often overlooked except during their brief afternoon opening. Both share the same punctual blooming habit and similar leaf arrangement.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Marvel of Peru is much more commonly grown than its wild relative, Wild Four O'Clock, which has smaller, less showy flowers and grows naturally in prairie regions.
